When the goal price keeps rising: compare the saving balance with the bill you will actually pay

Follow two growing paths, solve the monthly contribution and test how a later deadline changes both the time available and the price of the goal.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow a saving balance beside a changing goal price

Interactive planning lab

Goal price at the selected deadline$73,872.77
Monthly contribution required from now$565.84
Unfunded amount at the deadline$7,121.35

Original hypothetical fixed-quantity goal, priced in nominal CAD. The goal price rises at the entered constant effective annual rate, compounded proportionally across months. The saving account earns its own constant effective annual return converted monthly; contributions arrive at month-end after growth. Starting savings belong exclusively to this goal. The solver uses the same horizon, rates and payment timing and floors the required contribution at zero when starting funds already cover the modeled target. No withdrawals, fees, tax, account contribution limits, uncertain returns, price volatility, credit or changes in the goal quantity are modeled. The goal-price increase is not a forecast for homes, tuition or consumer prices. All alternative deadlines reprice the goal at their own date.

The central idea

A larger saving balance does not by itself establish progress toward an affordable goal. Compare the account and the goal price at the same future date, using separately stated assumptions.

01

A target amount needs a date as well as a number

A saving plan can pass an old target while still falling short of the purchase it was meant to fund. The account may have grown, but the cost of the same goal may have changed too. A comparison with the original price answers a different question from a comparison with the bill due at the planned purchase date.

The FCAC’s goal-setting guidance pairs an amount with a timeframe and recommends reviewing the plan. This guide extends that planning structure by giving the goal price and the saving account separate growth assumptions.

The goal is a fixed quantity: the same underlying purchase throughout the illustration. Its price increases at a constant assumed rate. An actual family may instead reduce the scope, choose another supplier or change the purchase. Those are useful decisions, but they should be recorded as changes to the goal rather than silently hidden inside an assumed investment return.

02

Read the price and saving paths together

Restore the example to start with a CAD 50,000 goal, CAD 10,000 already assigned to it and CAD 500 added at every month-end for eight years. The goal price is assumed to increase by 5% annually. The saving account earns a separate assumed 3% effective annual return.

At the deadline, the account holds about CAD 66,751.42. That is more than the original CAD 50,000 target, but the modeled goal now costs about CAD 73,872.77. The shortfall is about CAD 7,121.35. Using today’s price as the future target would incorrectly describe this particular plan as fully funded.

The line chart places both amounts on one nominal-CAD scale and the same calendar. The account receives monthly contributions after that month’s growth. The goal price uses proportional monthly compounding of its annual assumption. Neither line is a forecast or a quotation. Their purpose is to make the consequences of the chosen assumptions visible.

03

Solve the contribution without treating it as an investment return

The required-transfer calculation first grows the starting balance to the deadline. It then asks how much of the future goal remains to be funded by new monthly contributions. Each earlier contribution has more months to grow than a later one.

With monthly account rate r and n contributions, the accumulated value of one dollar contributed at each month-end is ((1 + r)n − 1) ÷ r. The required monthly transfer is the remaining future funding need divided by that factor. When the account return is zero, the factor is simply n. If starting funds alone already cover the modeled goal, the required new contribution is zero.

At the default settings, the solved monthly amount is about CAD 565.84, rather than CAD 500. The calculation uses unrounded values internally; displayed cents can leave a small rounding difference if used as an actual standing instruction. A transfer also needs to fit the household budget and the rules of the chosen account. The solver does not establish either affordability or available registered-account contribution room.

04

A longer wait changes both sides of the plan

The deadline bars solve separate two-, five-, eight- and twelve-year plans. Every case starts with the same assigned savings and the same current goal price. Each future date receives its own accumulated account value and its own repriced goal.

Extra time creates more contribution dates and more opportunity for account growth. It also exposes the goal to more assumed price increases. The resulting required monthly amount reflects both effects. It should not be interpreted as a comparison that keeps the future purchase price fixed while only adding saving years.

Under some combinations of a fast-growing price and a lower account return, extending a sufficiently distant deadline may stop reducing the required monthly amount. This is a property of those assumptions, not a prediction that waiting is always harmful. The appropriate response is to review the goal, saving capacity and timing together. Raising the return assumption solely to make an unaffordable plan appear funded leaves the underlying uncertainty unresolved.

05

Reconcile the gap before deciding how to close it

The waterfall starts with today’s CAD 50,000 goal and adds about CAD 23,872.77 of modeled price increase. It subtracts the CAD 10,000 starting balance, CAD 48,000 of new contributions and about CAD 8,751.42 of account growth. The endpoint is the same CAD 7,121.35 shortfall shown above.

This separates the household’s contribution effort from the account’s return. The CAD 48,000 is not a gain earned by the investment; it is new money the household supplied. Similarly, the increase in the target is not a loss inside the account. It is a change in the price of the separate goal.

If accumulated funds exceed the target, the waterfall retains a negative endpoint to show the surplus. The headline instead reports zero unfunded amount. Those displays use different sign conventions for different purposes, so the surplus should not be added back to the account a second time.

06

Keep the plan tied to supported prices and usable cash

The matrix changes goal-price growth and the account return independently. It holds the starting price, starting balance and deadline selected in the tool. Every cell solves the full monthly transfer under that combination. The cells are scenarios, not confidence intervals, success rates or recommendations for particular investments.

For an actual plan, replace the starting cost with a dated, relevant estimate and record what it includes. Check whether deposits are due before the final purchase date; a single deadline cannot represent an earlier payment schedule. Confirm which savings are exclusively assigned to this goal rather than also required for an emergency reserve or another bill.

Review the price and the account at consistent intervals. A real target can change abruptly, while account returns can be uneven or negative. This simple tool excludes those paths, taxes and fees. Its practical contribution is a repeatable funding question: at the date the money is needed, how much does the goal cost, how much is actually assigned to it, and what saving commitment closes the supported gap?
